sentences.text: From question to study plan: design, sample size, consent, and the I R B for a biometric ad study
This last workshop starts before any data exist.
A client asks, "Which of our ads should we run, and does the brand matter?"
It ends with a complete study plan that the instructor, the I R B, and the lab can review before the first participant is contacted.
Every section explains why before how.

Planning a study is a chain of decisions, and each one limits the next: the comparison that answers the question, the design that decides who sees what and in which order, the stimuli and sensors, the sample size with its justification, the counterbalancing, the exclusion rules and the analysis plan written before data, the informed consent form, the application to the Institutional Review Board (I R B), the session plan and staffing, and a pilot.
The idea that holds them together: a study is designed backward from the decision it must support and forward from the lab's real capacity.
Workshop 9 also closes the loop of the series.

Workshop 8 ended with a list of what the next study needs: more participants, several ads per brand, purchase intention asked separately for each brand, a smallest difference named in advance, and a plan fixed before data collection.
Section 03 turns that list into a Planned follow up study for the fictional brands Altavo and Brenlow, and the later sections build, justify, and staff it.
All of its numbers are simulated or Planned; no person was recorded.
If you start here, section 03 recaps Workshops 7 and 8 on one page and the data folder holds every file.
Read this workshop before you propose any study of your own in the lab.
Time needed.

About 5 hours over two sittings: sections 01 to 05 (the question, the design, the worked example, the iMotions build, and consent and the I R B) in the first, 06 to 10 (sensors, sample size, the analysis plan, sessions and the pilot, and the checklist) in the second

No participant before the I R B says yes The lab procedure manual (section 2.1) requires an I R B application "for any study to be run in the lab" and I R B "approval (or exemption) before scheduling participants."
J S U's I R B application form says the same from the other side: "Start date cannot predate I R B approval".
In this workshop everything up to the I R B submission is planning on paper; recruitment, the pilot, and every session come after approval.
J S U's pages and forms change, and the I R B office (I R B at J S U dot E D U) is the authority; section 05 shows what J S U's own pages say.
Nothing here is legal advice: the I R B decides.
Say what planning a study covers, place the Planned follow up study after Workshop 8, and state the rule that no participant is contacted before the I R B approves or exempts the study.
From question to comparison
A client does not bring a research question; it brings a decision.
The fictional Altavo brand team asks, "Which of our ads should we run, and does the brand matter?"
The first half is about particular ads, the second about every ad the brand might run, and no single measurement answers either.
"Better" can mean seen, felt, liked, or remembered, and "does the brand matter" needs a comparison in which the brand is the only systematic difference.
The first job of planning is translation: from the decision to a research question, from the question to a comparison, and from the comparison to hypotheses written before any data exist.

The iMotions article Designing Your Research Study makes this its first step (figure in section 00): "Determine the core of what your target client is trying to answer and think about the business impact of what they are asking.
In other words, dive deeper and avoid taking the objective from a research brief at face value."

It also asks what can be controlled, "such as the number of stimuli or variables, or the environment," and reminds the researcher that "clients desire ecological validity for their research results": the study should resemble the real situation closely enough for the answer to matter.
"A research question identifies your main problem or question you are aiming to answer and signals what type of study you need to conduct."
The article's table (figure below) lists what separates a good research question from a bad one.
A good one identifies the variables, is quantifiable and measurable, names the materials and the population, and asks what or how.
A bad one is opinion based, too general, silent about materials or population, answerable with yes or no, or too simple to test.
The client's "Which ad should we run?"
fails on most counts, exactly like the table's "What kind of TV ad is the best?"
The lab's study type guide (Project doc 01) adds a one sentence test.

A usable comparison names "who (the population), sees what (the stimuli and conditions), measured how (the sensor and metric), compared against what (the other condition, a baseline, or a benchmark)."

For the follow up study it reads: adults (the age limit the I R B approves) see six Altavo and six Brenlow video ads of 30 seconds, one participant at a time; each rates liking from 1 to 7 after every ad; and the Altavo ads are compared against the Brenlow ads, with the ads treated as a sample of each brand's possible ads.
The planning checklist turns that into one question, "Is Altavo advertising liked more than Brenlow advertising, beyond the particular ads?"
, and adds the smallest difference that would matter: 0.50 points on the 1 to 7 scale (Planned, a decision of the fictional client).
Naming that number before the data exist gives the sample size justification a target, and section 07 builds on it.
A comparison can answer a question only if the conditions differ in one respect.
Anything else that changes with the condition is a confound, a rival explanation for any difference you find.
Shadish, Cook, and Campbell treat such rival explanations as threats to internal validity; the classic remedies are to hold other variables constant and to let chance decide who gets which condition.
The vendor's own example (figure below) asks about music.
The good design uses "6 versions of same visual creative, with different music in each," because "By holding the visual creative constant, we isolate the effect of just music."

The less optimal design uses "6 different ads, with different variations of music, visual style, and story," and the article names the flaw: "Changing multiple variables within the same test makes it impossible to isolate the effect of any one variable."
Workshops 7 and 8 had the less optimal shape.
Ad A (Altavo, a hiking scene) and Ad B (Brenlow, a cycling scene) differed in brand, scene, sport, and every detail of the execution at once.

Workshop 8 found liking higher for Ad A by 0.55 points, 95 percent confidence interval -0.13 to 1.23 (simulated), and its discussion said why even a clear difference would not have settled the brand question: "Only one ad per brand was tested, so any difference between the ads cannot be separated from the particular executions."
If the client's question were whether the logo itself changes reactions, the cleanest comparison would hold one ad constant and swap the logo.

The client's question is about each brand's advertising, so the follow up study takes the other road: it samples several ads per brand, so that differences between executions average out and their spread can be measured (section 02).
"The changed or manipulated variables are the independent variables," and the outcome "that we want to measure" is the dependent variable (figure below).
An independent variable is set by the design; a dependent variable is recorded in response.

The article also sorts variables by how they are measured: a discrete variable can be counted ("number of children"), a continuous variable can take any value on a scale ("reaction time"), and the difference "has huge implications for designing the most appropriate study for your research question, and deciding on what statistical test to use."
The variables of the follow up study, from the model analysis plan (analysis plan prereg dot M D, section 4):
The last column carries a lesson from Workshop 8.
A measure answers a comparison only if it is taken at the level of that comparison, the unit of analysis.
Workshop 7 asked purchase intention once, after both ads, about reusable water bottles in general, so Workshop 8 could not compare the ads on it.
The follow up study asks it after each ad.
"A hypothesis is a testable answer to your research question.
It includes the specific variables that are going to be tested."

The article adds when to write it: "In scientific studies, hypotheses are generated before designing your study and collecting any data," which "prevents interpreting the results in line with your expectations, or confirmation bias" (figure below).
Its third step gives the commercial reason: "Try to avoid conducting studies 'just to see what we can see'.
Biometric measures are granular enough that you can almost always find some result, but without a specific business question, that result may just be found due to random chance."
(The article then points to a section on the multiple comparisons problem that it does not contain; Workshop 8, sections 01 and 06, covers families of tests.)
The research literature says the same with evidence.
Undisclosed flexibility in which measures, participants, and tests to report lets almost any data set produce a significant result (Simmons and colleagues
, 2011), and a plan written before the data separates prediction, which tests a hypothesis, from postdiction, which only suggests one.
The follow up study's hypotheses, all two tailed, are written in the model analysis plan:
P 1, primary: liking of the ads differs between the brands when ads are treated as a sample of each brand's possible ads.
Smallest effect of interest: 0.50 points.

S1 to S3, secondary family: purchase intention (S1), percent of time with Joy (S2), and G S R peaks per minute (S3) differ between the twelve Altavo and Brenlow ads shown, with Holm's correction over the three.

R 1 to R 3, replications of Workshop 7: brand recall is more likely when the Logo was fixated (R 1, Workshop 7 H 1); ads that produce more Joy in a participant are liked more by that participant (R 2, H 2); G S R peaks per minute are higher during the ads than during the Baseline (R 3, H 3).
The plan expects Altavo to be liked more, but only because Workshop 8 leaned that way with an interval that included zero, so the tests are two tailed and do not assume it.
One naming warning: the model plan uses R both for these replication hypotheses and for its exclusion rules R 1 to R 3.
This workshop always writes "replication R 1" or "rule R 1".
The fourth step of the scheme: "align hypotheses with deliverables.
Decide on the specific metrics you will use to answer each of your questions and which sensors are best to obtain the results you are looking for."
Each hypothesis needs a measure, a modality or source, an export that holds the number, and a result the report will show.
If a row cannot be filled, the hypothesis is not ready.
The table also shows what the study will not deliver.

There is no row for E E G: the Enobio 8's channel map is not yet configured on the lab computer, so the vendor's "Neural Approach and Avoid Response" deliverable (section 03) is left out rather than promised.

Translate a client's decision into a research question that names the population, materials, variables, and comparison; explain why a comparison must isolate one difference and why one ad per brand cannot answer a brand question; sort independent from dependent variables and say at what level each is measured; and write hypotheses before data and align each with a measure, a sensor, and a deliverable.
Choosing the design
With the comparison fixed, the design decides who sees which conditions and in what order.

Three choices follow, and each trades statistical power against session length and the risk of bias: between or within subjects, how the order of stimuli is handled, and how many stimuli represent each condition.
The follow up study makes all three choices for reasons this section spells out.
The iMotions article defines the two basic designs (figure below).
In a between subjects design, "the participants are assigned to only one of the independent variable's levels"; in a within subjects design, "all participants join all conditions of the study."
One sentence of the article has the labels backward: it calls the case in which participants "test all three websites" ("the former") between subjects.
The definitions that follow it are correct; learn those.
The article states the trade off plainly.
Between subjects: "the study sessions are shorter in duration.
However, a higher sample size is needed, since every respondent will join only one condition."

Within subjects: "typically cost less, since fewer participants are necessary," and "less error from confounding variables such as personality and mood, with each individual serving as their control," but "participants may become too tired and bored if you are testing too many conditions.
This exposure fatigue may alter the results of your study."
"Each individual serving as their control" is the reason the follow up study is within subjects.

In the Workshop 7 liking data, participants differed from one another with an standard deviation of 0.80 points, and one person's ratings of different ads varied around that person's own level with an standard deviation of 1.09 points (simulated; planning values A2 and A3 in simulated planning assumptions dot C S V).
When each person rates both brands, the person's own level cancels in the comparison; when different people rate each brand, those person to person differences stay in the error.
Greenwald weighed the same gain against its price, the context effects of within subjects designs: practice, sensitization to what is being compared, and carryover from one condition to the next.

Charness, Gneezy, and Kuhn reach a similar balance for experiments in economics: within subjects designs buy power, between subjects designs avoid the risk that seeing several conditions changes how people respond to each (Charness and colleagues
A mixed design puts one factor between and another within (figure below).
It fits when one factor cannot be undone: a participant who has used a phone cannot meet the websites fresh on a laptop, so the device goes between and the websites within.
In a within subjects design, every participant meets the conditions in some order, and order can change the results.
An order effect is any influence of the sequence on the responses.
Two kinds matter here.

A position effect depends on where in the session a stimulus falls: early items meet a fresh viewer, late ones a tired one, and the Cognitive Principles Guide notes that "object recall is greatest for the first and last items in an experience."
A carryover effect depends on what came just before: "if A and B co-occur, they are learned together and B may take on some of the 'negative' aspects of A."
The iMotions article's answer is randomization (figure below): "If the order of stimuli is randomized for each participant, these effects would cancel each other out when results are aggregated.
This procedure is called counterbalancing."
The difference matters for a study of 48 people and 12 ads.
With random orders, chance alone will put some ads early more often than others, and a brand whose ads happen to come first more often gains or loses from it.
Counterbalancing in the strict sense removes that chance.
A Latin square is a set of orders, one per row, in which every condition appears once in every position.
A Williams design is a Latin square chosen so that every condition is also immediately followed by every other condition exactly once, which balances first order carryover as well.
Brooks explains why an ordinary Latin square balances position but not which condition comes just before which, and how designs of this kind handle carryover.
In plain words.
Read the square for four ads, A to D, the one that step 5 of plan power dot R builds and checks.
Down each column (position) every ad appears once, so no ad is always first.
Along the rows, the twelve neighbor pairs AB, BD, DC, BC, CA, AD, CD, DB, BA, DA, AC, and CB each occur once, so every ad follows every other ad exactly once.
Give each row to the same number of participants, and position and first order carryover are spread evenly over the ads.

Brands add one more requirement.
In the follow up square the ads are labeled so that no row shows more than two ads of one brand in a row (brand pattern Abba...
or Baab...)
, every position holds an Altavo ad in 6 of the 12 rows, and 24 participants start with each brand (Planned, plan output dot T X T, step 5).
Section 04 builds the order in iMotions and reproduces the square in Excel (section 4.6).
The iMotions tools match these designs closely, though not by the same names.

The Test Plan article shows four exposure orders (figure below): "Monadic Design," in which "each respondent will only be exposed to one stimulus," is a between subjects design; "Completely Randomised Design" is a random order per respondent; "Randomized Block Design" groups stimuli into blocks; and "Cell Design," in which one cell of people "tests Product A first and then Product B, while the other subsample (cell) tests the two products in reverse order," is the AB and BA counterbalancing of Workshops 7 and 8.
The table maps each design to the tools of the Study Builder and the Test Plan, as the 2023 manuals describe them.
A study flow is one version of a study's sequence ("Only one flow will be shown per respondent"); a Test Plan is a study created from a C S V file of respondents and their stimulus sequences.
Whether every label below still reads the same in iMotions Lab 11 point 1 is on the Items to verify list (section 11); section 04 builds the follow up design step by step.
Ads do not only follow each other; they also teach the viewer.

The Cognitive Principles Guide (figure below) describes the mere exposure effect: "Even a single, brief exposure to a stimulus is enough for individuals to form an affective preference relative to an unfamiliar stimulus."
In a session of 12 ads, a participant's fifth Altavo ad is not a first meeting with the brand, and liking may drift up with each exposure.
The Williams order cannot stop that drift, but it makes sure it cannot favor one brand: across the rows both brands hold the same positions equally often and start equally often.
Other principles in the guide are rules for matching stimuli before collection.

Familiar items show "improved recall" and novel items "improved recognition," so a familiar real brand and a new one differ before any ad plays; the two fictional brands of the worked example start level, but a client's real brands may not.

The guide also notes that "information-heavy creative is less likely to connect emotionally with individuals," so an informational Altavo campaign against an emotional Brenlow campaign would mix style with brand.
Such differences are not mistakes if the client wants to compare the campaigns as they are, but the report must then say that the brands differ in style as well as name.
Participants are a sample from a population of people, and every analysis in Workshops 7 and 8 treated them that way.
The ads are a sample as well, from all the ads a brand could run, and a claim about a brand's advertising is a claim about that population.
When a category is represented by one stimulus, every feature of that stimulus is tied to the category; stimulus sampling, several stimuli per category, is the remedy.
The analysis must then treat the ads, like the participants, as a random factor, and the claim must not reach further than the variation the model includes.
This has a surprising consequence for planning.
When ads are random, the brand difference is judged against how much the ads of one brand differ from each other, and that spread is estimated from the ads, not from the people.
Power then depends on the number of ads as well as the number of participants, and adding participants cannot make up for too few ads.

The planning simulation shows it (simulated; a 0.50 point brand difference in liking, ads of one brand differing with an standard deviation of 0.20 points, 500 simulated studies per cell): with 3 ads per brand, power was point 4 7 4 at 48 participants and only point 5 1 0 at 72; with 6 ads per brand it was point 8 8 0 at 48.
Section 07 shows the whole grid and how much the result depends on the assumed spread of the ads.
The vendor's good design used six examples too: "6 examples is typically sufficient to control for creative effects."
The two sixes agree, but they are not the same kind of number.

The vendor's six is a rule of thumb; the plan's six is the smallest of the numbers simulated (2, 3, 4, and 6 ads per brand) that reached point 8 0 power in a simulation of the planned test under stated assumptions, and it would change if those assumptions did.

Twelve ads also lengthen the session, the exposure fatigue the article warns about; the recording takes 15.7 minutes by the plan's arithmetic (Planned as 20), the Williams order spreads fatigue evenly over both brands, and the pilot measures the real length (section 09).

Choose between, within, and mixed designs and name what each costs; tell position from carryover effects; distinguish a random order from a counterbalanced one and say what a Latin square and a Williams design balance; map each design to the iMotions tool that builds it; and explain why a brand claim needs several ads per brand and why the number of ads limits power.
The worked example
Everything in sections 01 and 02 fits on one page.

Below are the story so far for readers who start here, what Workshop 8 asked the next study to do, the follow up study as a one page plan, the files that hold every decision, and where the plan departs from the vendor's template.
Read it as a model for your own plan; section 10 turns it into a checklist.
A Planned study with simulated planning data No person was recorded and no participant was contacted.
Every power value was computed from simulated data sets (plan power.

R, seed 20270208); every planning value comes from the simulated study of Workshops 7 and 8 (seed 20271231) or is labeled a judgment; every date is a placeholder; participants and staff carry codes only (P 01, R 01, X01; S1 to S6).
Altavo and Brenlow are invented brands, and the Altavo brand team is a fictional client.
The consent form in the data folder is a Teaching Model: it must be replaced by the current J S U I R B template and approved by the I R B before any use.
No number in this section may be quoted as a finding.
Workshop 7 recorded a simulated study.

Twenty-four participants (P 01 to P 24) came to the lab one at a time and saw an instruction screen, a 60 seconds Baseline (a gray screen with a fixation cross), and two 30 seconds ads for reusable water bottles: Ad A for Altavo, a hiking scene, and Ad B for Brenlow, a cycling scene.
Odd participants saw the order AB and even participants BA, and a survey followed.
A Smart Eye Aurora tracked gaze at 60 hertz on three A O I's per ad (Logo, Product, Headline), aff decks scored the face, and a Shimmer 3 G S R plus recorded skin conductance.
Three exclusion rules written before collection left 22 participants.

Workshop 8 found that both ads raised G S R above the Baseline (d z equals 0.83 and 0.95), that attention followed the same hierarchy in both ads, and that viewers who fixated the Logo were more likely to recall the brand (odds ratio equals 4.34).
The ads did not differ detectably in liking (0.55 points, 95 percent confidence interval -0.13 to 1.23), recall, or arousal.
The design could not have told: 22 paired observations detect only d z of 0.63 or more, and with one ad per brand any difference mixes brand and execution.

What the next study needs (Workshop 8, results text dot M D) "To detect a moderate difference between two ads on a paired measure (d z equals 0.50) with 80 percent power, the next study needs at least 34 participants for a single test and 45 if three measures are corrected as a Holm family ...
H 1 needs about 72 independent observations ...

The next study should also present several ads per brand so that brand effects can be separated from executions, ask purchase intention separately for each brand so that the ads can be compared on it, fix every question and its test in a preregistration before data collection (Nosek and colleagues
, 2018), and name in advance the smallest difference that would matter to the client, so that a null result can be tested for equivalence rather than left uninterpretable."
Each request has an answer in the plan (all Planned or simulated):
Which of our ads should we run, and does the brand matter?
The fictional Altavo brand team wants to know whether its advertising is liked more than Brenlow's, beyond the two ads of Workshops 7 and 8.
Is Altavo advertising liked more than Brenlow advertising, beyond the particular ads?
Smallest difference that matters: 0.50 points on the 1 to 7 liking scale (a decision of the fictional client).
P 1, primary: liking differs between the brands, ads random.
S1 to S3, secondary family with Holm over three: purchase intention, Joy, and G S R peaks per minute differ between the twelve ads shown.
Replications R 1 to R 3: Workshop 7 H 1 to H 3.
All two tailed.
Lab experiment, within subjects: every participant sees every ad.
Brand is a within subjects factor; ad is a random factor nested in brand; position (1 to 12) is counterbalanced.

Twelve 30 seconds video ads from the client, six per brand, each brand's six from one campaign, equal in length and resolution, with the same layout so that the Logo (top left), Product (center), and Headline (bottom) A O I's sit in the same place in every ad.
Whether the client can supply six comparable ads per brand is on the Items to verify list (section 11).
Smart Eye Aurora (60 hertz; one unit, so one participant at a time), aff decks on the respondent camera, and one Shimmer 3 G S R plus on two fingers, recorded in iMotions Lab 11 point 1.
Eye Tracking Screen based, aff decks, and Shimmer are on both license keys; confirm the modules on the computer used.

Consent and screening (about 15 min), sensor setup and calibration (about 10 min), recording (about 20 min: instructions, the 60 seconds Baseline, the 12 ads in the participant's order, two questions after each ad, end questions), sensors off and debriefing (about 15 min).

Liking and purchase intention (1 to 7) after each ad; brand recall for each ad at the end; Logo fixated and dwell on the three A O I's; Joy, Engagement, and Brow Furrow, percent of time at or above the threshold; G S R peaks per minute during the Baseline and each ad; attitude toward reusable water bottles (three items); age and gender; data quality.
48 participants who meet the rules, 576 ratings of liking.

Simulated power for P 1 is point 8 8 0 (Monte Carlo standard error point 0 1 5, the uncertainty of the simulation itself) for a 0.50 point brand difference if ads of one brand differ with an standard deviation of 0.20 points, a judgment because no lab estimate exists; at an standard deviation of 0.30, power falls to point 6 4 0.
Simulated Type I error of the planned test: point 0 5 2.
Forty-eight also covers the secondary family (45 at the strictest Holm step) and is a multiple of the 12 rows of the Williams design.
Stop when 48 participants meet exclusion rules R 1 and R 2, or after 60 sessions, whichever comes first.
53 sessions are booked (48 main and 5 reserve) plus 2 open slots.
A Williams design for 12 ads: each ad once in every position, each ad immediately after every other ad once, at most two ads of one brand in a row.
Participants P 01 to P 48 are assigned to rows in 4 blocks of 12; a reserve participant takes the row of the person replaced.
Rule R 1: use only recordings the session log marks for use.
Rule R 2: exclude and replace a participant whose session ended before the last ad, or whose eye tracking quality is below 90 percent, or face quality below 80 percent, on 3 or more of the 12 ads.
Rule R2b: for a kept participant, an ad below either threshold is missing for that sensor's measures.
Rule R 3: G S R for a stimulus is missing when the signal covers less than 80 percent of it.
P 1: a mixed model, liking is modeled by brand + (1 given participant) + (1 given ad), with the brand difference judged against the variation between ads.
S1 to S3: paired t tests of each participant's Altavo minus Brenlow mean, Holm over three.
Replications: mixed logistic model (R 1), mixed model (R 2), paired t test (R 3).
Exploratory analyses E1 to E6, labeled as such in advance.

Adults only; about 60 minutes; says what each sensor records, that the face video identifies the person, where data are kept, who sees them, and for how long; optional permissions, with face clips shown only after a separate written release.
The model form is a Teaching Model that must be replaced by the current J S U template and approved by the I R B.

Approval or exemption before anyone is scheduled; the approval letter and approved consent form on file; the I R B number in the lab logbook; current citty training for everyone who collects data; an amendment for any change, "even seemingly minor ones (such as adding a questionnaire)" (lab procedure manual, section 2.1).
The review level is the I R B's decision (section 05).
60 minutes of participant time in 90 minute slots (the extra 30 minutes for backup, the session log, and cleaning), 5 slots per weekday, two trained staff per session, 55 slots on 11 weekdays.
Placeholder dates: February 8 to 22, 2027, set only after I R B approval.
Two sessions (codes X01 and X02) on a pilot day one week earlier (placeholder: February 1, 2027); the data are checked, not analyzed.

Go if both finish within 60 minutes, the Aurora calibrates, eye tracking quality is at least 90 percent and face quality at least 80 percent on the pilot ads, G S R shows peaks, and every export opens in the planned pipeline.

The brand comparison P 1 with its interval (and the equivalence test if it is not significant), the secondary family S1 to S3 for the client report, an ad by ad description (E4: mean and 95 percent confidence interval of liking, purchase intention, Joy, and recall for each ad, without tests), and the replications.

All files sit in the site's data folder; the read me says what each is, how to run the script (about 9 minutes on one core, or about 2.5 minutes in its quick mode, whose numbers differ slightly), and which results look like errors but are not.

From Workshop 7: the planning values for liking (participant standard deviation 0.80, residual standard deviation 1.09), the exclusion rate (2 of 24), the 90 minute slots (the median gap between session starts was 91 minutes), the measures and A O I's, rules R 1 to R 3 adapted to twelve ads, and the session log columns.

From Workshop 8: the paired sample sizes, reproduced exactly as a continuity check; the planning values for replication R 1 (recall point 3 5 when the Logo is not fixated; odds ratio 4.34); and the requests in the box above.
From Workshop 6: remote studies lose far more people.
Of 260 who opened the link, 142 were kept, so the same 48 analyzable participants would need about 88 link openers; one more reason to run the follow up in the lab.

The vendor's TV and Digital Ad Testing template (figure below) lists the objective this study serves, "Understand which, of multiple, creatives may perform best in-market," and two sample specifications the plan does not follow.
"N equals 30 per cell" is a recruiting convention, not a power analysis; the plan's 48 comes from a simulation of the planned test.
"Up to 3 videos per person" is exceeded on purpose: showing each participant twelve ads is what gives the brand test its power (section 02).

The plan pays for it with a longer recording (15.7 minutes computed, 20 planned), balances fatigue and familiarity across brands with the Williams order, checks position as an exploratory analysis, and lets the pilot measure the real length.
"100 percent right-handed (for E E G)" does not apply, because the study records no E E G.
Twelve ads raise one more question that the model plan does not yet answer: are the ads alike in pacing?
The Cognitive Principles Guide (figure below) warns that cuts "under one second" tax the viewer and often reduce emotional response.
If one brand's campaign is cut faster than the other's, a brand difference in Joy or G S R could be a difference in editing.
A reviewer could reasonably ask the team to compare the pacing of the twelve ads before the I R B submission, or to describe it in the report.
A stopping rule says in advance when data collection ends.
The follow up study's rule (analysis plan prereg dot M D, section 3.5): "Data collection stops when 48 participants meet rules R 1 and R 2 ...
or after 60 sessions (25 percent above the target), whichever comes first."

Consent, the I R B, and recruitment
A biometric ad study records people: where their eyes go, how their skin responds, and a video of their face.

Three things must be in place before anyone is recruited: a decision of the Institutional Review Board (I R B), a consent form that says exactly what is recorded, stored, and shared, and a recruitment plan that leaves people free to say no.

The lab procedure manual makes the first a rule: "All research conducted in the Consumer Behavior Lab must have prior approval from the Jacksonville State University Institutional Review Board (I R B)", obtained "(or exemption) before scheduling participants" (section 2.1).

The Belmont Report of April 18, 1979 names "three basic principles": "respect of persons, beneficence and justice"; read it on the H H S Belmont Report page.

Respect for persons means that "individuals should be treated as autonomous agents"; beneficence means "(1) do not harm and (2) maximize possible benefits and minimize possible harms"; justice asks who should bear the burdens of research.

Consent has "three elements: information, comprehension and voluntariness", and two things undermine voluntariness: coercion, "an overt threat of harm", and undue influence, "an offer of an excessive, unwarranted, inappropriate or improper reward".

In an ad study, respect means telling people about the face video before they agree, beneficence means keeping skin, eye, and privacy risks small, and justice means not choosing participants "solely for administrative convenience", such as the students of your own class (section 5.7).
Why.

The federal rules for human research, 45 C F R 46, say what informed consent must contain, and J S U applies the regulations "to all research and research-related activities that involve human subjects".

The e C F R text of 45 C F R 46 point 116 asks for "language understandable to the subject" and for a start with key information: "Informed consent must begin with a concise and focused presentation of the key information that is most likely to assist a prospective subject or legally authorized representative in understanding the reasons why one might or might not want to participate in the research."
The basic elements, condensed (the O H R P page Basic Elements of Informed Consent explains them), with the part of the Teaching Model consent form of section 5.

Under 46 point 117, consent is documented "by the use of a written informed consent form approved by the I R B", and "A written copy shall be given to the person signing".

The A P A Ethics Code requires consent before voices or images are recorded for data collection (Standard 8.03), and the N M S B A Code of Ethics asks researchers to "explain the tools they use to participants in layman terms" and never to reveal a participant's identity "to the client without explicit consent" (Neuromarketing Science and Business Association, n dot d.)

A form alone does not ensure understanding: in a systematic review, more time talking one to one with a member of the study team improved understanding more consistently than changes to the written form, and the lab procedure manual likewise asks you to "Answer all questions the participant has before proceeding" (section 2.2).
Why.

The iMotions consent F A Q lists what "you must be able to document that you informed the respondent about": the purpose, that participation is voluntary, the respondent's rights, how the data are handled, and the possible risks (figure below).

The lab's rule: "Facial video is identifiable data: say so in the consent form, store it under the retention rules, and never publish a participant's face without written release" (Project doc 01).

J S U's application asks the same of any study that records video: "clearly indicate if the information is identifiable and what steps will be taken to protect the confidentiality of the participants".
List what is recorded before writing a word: gaze data, the face video, any sound, the screen, the survey answers, with where each is stored, who can see it, and when it is deleted.

With iMotions Lab "all data will be stored locally on your PC", which must be protected "with a password and encryption"; with a cloud product "you will also need to declare to the respondent where their data will be stored and processed".
The respondent camera settings on the lab computer include an "Include Audio" option; decide for each study whether sound is needed, because "the voice can identify the respondent" (Items to verify).

Readability.

The J S U application says that consent documents "must be written at an appropriate level for participants and follow the J S U template": "for the general population, no higher than an 8th grade level; for college students, no higher than a 12th grade level", and "The I R B will verify readability using a Flesch Kincaid Grade Level as measured in MS Word".
The model is written for an eighth grade reader.
Which J S U document?

The application says to follow "the J S U template", but the I R B page offers two checklists rather than a template: the Informed Consent Statement Checklist for adults and the Informed Consent Statement Checklist for Minors (both read October 2026).
Confirm with the I R B office which one to follow.

Comparing the model with the adult checklist is a good exercise: the checklist asks for a "Funding Declaration", which the model lacks, and says that "anything collected prior to withdrawal will be removed from the study", a point the model leaves to the I R B.
Why.
Research with children needs two agreements.

Subpart D of the federal rules (45 C F R 46 Subpart D) defines permission as "the agreement of parent(s) or guardian to the participation of their child or ward in research" and assent as "a child's affirmative agreement to participate in research.
Mere failure to object should not, absent affirmative agreement, be construed as assent."

The I R B decides whether children can give assent, taking into account "the ages, maturity, and psychological state of the children involved" (46 point 408(a)), and "may find that the permission of one parent is sufficient" for minimal risk research and for one other category of research named in 46 point 408(b).
What a child can understand changes with age, so assent procedures have to fit the child; the Institute of Medicine's report on research with children treats permission and assent together.
What J S U's pages add (read October 2026).
The I R B page: "Any research involving children under 14 years of age must have full board review."

The checklist for minors has a parent signature block but no assent wording, and the N M S B A code (Article 8) requires the consent of parents or legal guardians for participants under 18.
Federal rules leave the age of consent to local law (46 point 402(a)), so the age at which a J S U participant may consent alone is a question for the I R B office (Items to verify).

The I R B page (read October 2026) defines minimal risk as "harm or discomfort of no greater probability and magnitude than those ordinarily encountered in daily life" and sorts research into "exempt, expedited, and all other": exempt for "very narrowly defined types of research" without vulnerable populations, expedited for "ten restricted types of research", and full board review for the rest: "All other research must be reviewed in full by the I R B."

J S U's I R B Application Form asks investigators to "Justify how the number of anticipated participants is reasonable for this research", and the reviewers' I R B Application Review Sheet asks "Are the number of participants justified?"
(both read October 2026).
A number chosen because it fills a class, or because the vendor usually recruits it, is not a justification.
A sample size justification states what the study must be able to detect and shows that the planned sample can do so.

Power by simulation has five steps, which plan power dot R writes out by hand so that each can be read:

The analysis plan and preregistration: deciding every test before the first participant
Workshop 8 tested three hypotheses written before collection and four questions fixed after collection but before analysis, and it had to say that the second group "carry less confirmatory weight."
This section removes that gap.
The analysis plan of the follow up study names every hypothesis, rule, model, and correction before any data exist, and it is dated and frozen before the first participant is recorded.
The model is analysis plan prereg dot M D: a Planned study with simulated planning values, written as a teaching model for fictional brands.
Before a real study it must be completed with names, dates, and the approved I R B number, and it must agree with the protocol the J S U I R B approves.

The iMotions article Designing Your Research Study gives the vendor's version of the argument: setting hypotheses "before the study" keeps researchers and clients from "a 'fishing expedition'," because "Biometric measures are granular enough that you can almost always find some result," which "may just be found due to random chance."

Research on false positives makes the same point more formally: undisclosed choices made while collecting and analyzing data, such as when to stop, which participants to drop, and which measures to report, can make almost any result significant, which is why the rule for ending data collection should be decided before it begins (Simmons and colleagues
A preregistration separates prediction, a test written before the data, from postdiction, an explanation found in them; both are useful, but only the first can confirm a hypothesis.
The model follows the common structure of preregistration templates.
A template for social psychology (van 't Veer and Giner-Sorolla, 2016) and one from a joint task force of psychological societies for quantitative research (Bosnjak and colleagues
, 2022) ask for the same core: hypotheses, design, sampling, variables, analyses, and what happens to data that break the rules.
Each part answers a question a skeptical reader would ask (all Planned):

One label in the model looks like an error and is not: "R" names both the replication hypotheses (R 1 to R 3, the Workshop 7 hypotheses H 1 to H 3) and the exclusion rules (rules R 1 to R 3, as in Workshop 7).
Read the word before it: hypothesis R 1 or rule R 1.
P 1, the primary hypothesis.
Liking differs between the brands when the ads are treated as a sample of each brand's possible ads; the smallest effect size of interest is 0.50 points on the 1 to 7 scale.
It is the only test that can support a brand claim, because it judges the brand difference against the variation between ads (section 02).
S1 to S3, the secondary family.
Purchase intention (S1), percent of time with Joy (S2), and G S R peaks per minute (S3) differ between the Altavo ads and the Brenlow ads.
These treat the twelve ads as fixed: they describe the ads that were shown, which is what the client report needs, and they do not generalize to other ads.
Holm's correction over the three keeps the familywise error rate of this family at point 0 5, as in Workshop 8.
R 1 to R 3, the replications.

The three Workshop 7 hypotheses, each its own family: brand recall is more likely when the logo of that ad was fixated (R 1); ads that produce more Joy in a person are liked more by that person (R 2); G S R peaks are higher during the ads than during the baseline (R 3).

Everything else is an exploratory analysis and was labeled as one before the data existed: dwell by brand and A O I (E1), Engagement and Brow Furrow (E2), position and carryover (E3), ad level means for the client without tests (E4), correlations across modalities with intervals and no p values (E5, as Workshop 8's E1), and the sensitivity of S2 to the aff decks threshold (E6).
A planned analysis can confirm; an exploratory one can only suggest the next hypothesis.
The sample is 48 participants who meet the inclusion and quality rules, each seeing all 12 ads, so 576 liking ratings (Planned; the justification is section 07).
The stopping rule in full: data collection stops when 48 participants meet rules R 1 and R 2, or after 60 sessions, whichever comes first.
From the Workshop 7 exclusion rate of 2 in 24, 53 sessions are expected: 48 main and 5 reserve are booked, with 2 open slots for no shows.
Outcome variables are not analyzed before the stopping rule is met; after each session only the quality checks run.
If more than 3 participants of a block of 12 fail rule R 2, collection pauses to look for a procedural cause such as calibration, lighting, or seating.

An exclusion rule states, before any data exist, its level (a whole participant or one observation), the measure and its threshold, the source of the threshold, the analyses it applies to, and what happens next, such as a replacement.

The mixed model of P 1 is new to the series in one respect: it gives participants and ads each a random intercept, where the models of Workshops 7 and 8 had a random intercept for participants only, so a brand difference must stand out against how much the ads of one brand differ from each other.

The singular fit rule exists because the simulations in section 07 showed that accepting several hundred df after a singular fit makes the test too liberal; with the rule, the simulated false positive rate at this design was point 0 5 2 (simulated).

Ignoring a possible random slope for each person's own brand preference raised the simulated false positive rate only to point 0 6 0 (simulated), and the plan fits that slope as a robustness check.
Every deliverable needs its test.

Why two people?

The script calls the G S R device one "worn like a wristwatch"; the lab's Shimmer 3 G S R plus uses two finger electrodes.
Use the lab manual's plain explanation (2.2): the finger sensors measure tiny changes in skin perspiration, and the participant will not feel anything.

The overview must give the duration the consent form states, about 60 minutes for this study, not a figure copied from another script or example.
In the lab procedure manual's words (7.1.5): "Try not to exceed what was told in consent."
Consent and screening.

Give time to read, talk the form through, and answer every question; in a systematic review, more time spent talking one on one with participants appeared to be the most effective available way to improve their understanding of consent.
Two signed copies, one for the participant; then the screening questions on skin allergies, seizures or sensitivity to flashing light, and the fingers (lab procedure manual 2.2, 7.1.3).
Calibration.
Keep the vendor's lines ("Please follow the dot with your eyes"; do not move the chair or the monitor after calibration).
The Collecting Data article recommends "instructing respondents about the calibration procedure before you click 'Start Recording'."
Seat the participant about 60 cm (roughly 24 inches) from the Aurora (lab procedure manual 5.3.2), and tell the participant that he or she can stop at any time (7.1.4).

Instructions before the visit come from the consent form and the manual's participant preparation list (Appendix F): clean, dry hands with no lotion, no eye makeup, rings off if possible, and a reminder the day before (3.2).
The Operational Resources article (section 00) also lists a Screener Template, self report question templates, and a consent form template marked "Inspiration only."
Neither it nor the teaching model consent form of this workshop may be used as it stands: a consent form must be written on the current J S U I R B template and approved by the I R B before use.
Participants are not passive.
They look for cues to what the study is about and often try to behave as good participants should; Orne called the sum of those cues the demand characteristics of an experiment.
In an ad study the cues come from the consent form, the script, the operator, and the room.
The Designing article's consent advice draws the line: describe the purpose, modalities, and risks "without giving away any priming or critical information about the results or outcome of the study."
The follow up plan tells participants that the study is about reactions to water bottle ads, not what is expected (analysis plan 2.2).
In practice:
Say "view the content as you normally would," and never which brand is the client or which result is hoped for.
Do not announce the recall test before the ads.
The Cognitive Principles Guide notes that what we focus on decides what we notice (change blindness), so viewers told to remember brands would hunt for logos and change the eye tracking measures.
The recall instructions belong to the end questions.
Keep the operator out of the room during recording and observe through the control room (the lab has a one way mirror and an intercom; use the intercom "sparingly," 7.1.5).
The operators know the brands; the plan asks the team to decide whether they can be kept unaware of the expected direction and, if not, to say so in the report.
Keep client names and logos off forms, screens, and walls.
Whether people who know the plan, such as students of this course, may take part is an eligibility question for the I R B application.

If anything about the purpose is withheld, the I R B application must say so and justify it (its Section 7 asks whether deception is part of the design and how participants will be debriefed; J S U I R B Application Form, read October 2026), and the debriefing explains it (lab procedure manual 7.1.6).

The lab rule is the lab procedure manual: wipe surfaces before each session, wear gloves for electrodes, dispose of single use items, disinfect equipment that touched the participant, and leave the room empty for at least 10 minutes (3.4); wipe electrodes with 70 percent isopropyl alcohol and let them air dry for 5 minutes, clean eye tracker lenses with a microfiber cloth, and wipe frames with an alcohol wipe (Appendix E).
The iMotions article How to properly sanitize your data collection site between participants adds vendor detail, such as one strap per participant, washed after use.
Read it with two cautions.
It was written "In light of the current situation with Covid-19," so its masks, acrylic dividers, and distancing describe those conditions, not a rule for this lab.
And its glasses section covers the Pupil Invisible model, while the lab owns Pupil Labs Neon, whose own care instructions apply (Items to verify, section 11).
Where the article and the manual differ, the manual wins.
The room is part of the procedure too: about 70 to 72 degreesF, consistent moderate lighting, no direct sunlight, and an intercom tested before the first participant (lab procedure manual 3.2).
The iMotions Lab Space article, shown in section 10, adds a light or sign outside the door that shows testing is in progress, and a chair without wheels that does not spin.
A pilot is a small run of the whole procedure before the study, to find out whether it can be done as planned.
It is not a small version of the study.
Its effect estimates are too imprecise to plan the sample size on, and it should not be used to test hypotheses.

Thabane and colleagues advise setting the pilot's objectives and criteria for success in advance and reading the outcome as one of a few decisions: stop, continue with changes, or continue as planned.
Read their 2023 correction with the article: it changes the worked example in its section on sample size for pilot studies from at least 75 to at least 289 patients.
The lab's guide puts the minimum plainly: "run two people end to end, export the data, and confirm that the primary metric comes out before recruiting" (Project doc 01).
Two days before each session, the manual adds a test run of the script that checks that "stimuli are loaded correctly and the randomization works" (7.1.1).
Pilot participants are participants, so the pilot comes after I R B approval.

The N M S B A Code of Ethics (Neuromarketing Science and Business Association, n dot d.)

, at nmsba dot com/ethics, sets the floor for neuromarketing research: explain the tools to participants "in layman terms" (Article 5); "The identity of participants will not be revealed to the client without explicit consent," data are used only for the stated purpose, and personal information is not kept longer than the project requires (Article 6); participants may withdraw at any time (Articles 5 and 7); and studies with participants under 18 need the consent of parents or guardians (Article 8).

Writers on the ethics of neuromarketing raise the same concerns from several directions: protecting participants, especially vulnerable ones; claims about what brain and body measures reveal that go beyond the evidence; and the autonomy of the consumers the results are used on (Murphy and colleagues
, 2008; Stanton and colleagues, 2017; Ulman and colleagues, 2015).
For planning, that comes down to five commitments written before collection.

The client receives group results only, never names or faces, unless a participant has given explicit, separate permission for a stated use; the teaching model consent form goes further and promises that the client will never see a name or a face (a Teaching Model that must be replaced by the current J S U template and approved by the I R B before use).
The analysis plan is shared with the client and frozen before the data exist, so that a disappointing result cannot be reanalyzed into a pleasing one, and every planned test is reported (Workshop 8).
The client hears before collection what the design cannot answer, for example a brand claim with fewer than six ads per brand.

Sharing is settled in advance: the N M S B A code says the research data "will not be shared," while open science asks for fair data, so the consent form and the client agreement must say which applies.
Finally, the lab procedure manual requires I R B approval for all research conducted in the lab (2.1).
